judgments.reasoning_cat1: The suicide clause is badly fragmented but its operative content — no death proceeds where suicide occurs within 2 years of amounts having been "in effect" — turns on the vague phrase identifying which two-year period runs (from issue, from an increase, or from a replaced policy's date), and on "amounts of" insurance in effect less than 2 years. That is a nameable ambiguity that determines whether a suicide is covered at all, and it is the classic litigated term in a replacement-policy setting.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against the Incontestability provision (2 years after date of issue or 2 years after any increase) and against the Right to Return Policy pages that expressly contemplate this contract replacing an existing policy, the start date of the suicide period is genuinely unsettled across the instrument. Whether the replacement character of the policy shortens or restarts the contestable/suicide window is precisely the kind of whole-instrument tension a court would resolve.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The insuring agreement is a standard promise to pay death proceeds on due proof of death while the contract was in force; the only softness is "subject to its terms," which is ordinary incorporation language. OCR damage obscures words but the meaning is conventional and definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly made subject to the contract's other terms, so the suicide, grace-period and incontestability provisions harmonise with it rather than conflict. No specific inconsistency found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A 20-day free-look with refund of premiums is a definite, mechanical term; the text is garbled but the operative period and remedy are clear. Nothing here requires a choice between two readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits directly against the Notice to Policyholder pages giving 30 days (and 45 in PA) to return a policy that replaces an existing policy, so a reader must decide which period governs this replacement policy. That is a real, though probably reconcilable, tension worth some weight.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is only a truncated list of state abbreviations with the operative sentence lost to OCR; as it stands it states no rule at all. The fragment cannot be construed, though a list of specified states raises an expressio unius question about unlisted states.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its relationship to the 20-day right-to-cancel page and to the other state-specific return blocks is the only live issue, and this jurisdiction's policy would have to be slotted into one block. Some tension, but nothing squarely contradictory.
judgments.clause_name: Right to Return Policy - AR, CT, DC, DE, FL etc.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rule is definite: if the policy replaces an existing policy, a 30-day return for full refund. "Replaces an existing policy" is a term that could be argued over, but it is a defined industry concept and the clause is otherwise plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It differs from the 20-day general right to cancel elsewhere in the contract, and the state lists across the several blocks do not obviously cover every jurisdiction. That leaves a modest reconciliation question rather than a flat conflict.
judgments.clause_name: Right to Return Policy - AL, AZ, CO, IA, KY, VA, UT, VT, WV

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The California block states a 30-day return right for a replacement policy in capitals; the wording is a straightforward conditional. No named term is genuinely two-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Same relationship to the 20-day cancellation page as the other state blocks, and it applies only to CA-issued policies, so it is unlikely to bite here. Low relational risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The PA block is the most heavily damaged, leaving "than v US,. or W" and a 45-day period conditioned on an unreadable clause; what triggers the 45 days cannot be read off the text. That is a genuine mechanical/vagueness defect on the face of the fragment.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sets a different period from both the 20-day cancellation page and the 30-day replacement blocks, so a PA-issued replacement policy would require choosing among them. Moderate relational tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Risk Class definition and the Table of Guaranteed Maximum Renewal Premiums. No conflict identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Identical disclaimer footnote repeated on the continued specifications page; definite boilerplate. No ambiguous term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicates neg7 and matches the Risk Class provision; harmless repetition rather than inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It squares with the Reinstatement, Beneficiary and Assignment provisions requiring written notice. No conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line definition of "Option" as payment of proceeds other than in one sum; truncated but conventional. Nothing genuinely two-sided.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The pronoun definition distinguishes owner from insured, but the OCR scrambling leaves the mapping of "you" partly unreadable. As drafted the concept is standard and definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with the rider's own "You, Your, or Yours" definition, which defines the same words for the rider; the rider expressly controls where it differs, so the overlap is managed. Low relational risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Requires proof of insurability "acceptable to us" and provides no new benefit takes effect until approval; "acceptable to us" is a discretionary standard courts sometimes qualify by good faith. Mild vagueness only.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Reinstatement and Conversion provisions, the latter of which waives evidence of insurability. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only the fragment "Unless we adopt other rules, your risk" survives, so no rule is stated; the defect is missing text rather than competing meanings. Very little to construe as written.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Grace Period, Renewal and Table of Guaranteed Maximum Renewal Premiums. No inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A 31-day grace period with the contract ending as of the premium due date and any due premium deducted from death proceeds; the terms are specific and dated. The only oddity is termination relating back to the due date, which is standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interacts with the Reinstatement provision and with the insuring agreement's "while the contract was in force," and the retroactive termination date could matter for a death during grace — but the clause itself resolves that. Low but not negligible.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Renewal each year on payment of the premium then due, with no renewal past the final term date on page 3; definite and cross-referenced. No ambiguous term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The referenced page 3 specifications do not legibly show a final term date, and the renewal table runs to 2049; that is a minor cross-reference gap rather than a contradiction. Low relational risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A three-condition reinstatement list (apply, we approve, pay past-due premiums) truncated by OCR; the structure is enumerated and definite. Nothing genuinely ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Grace Period and Proof You Can Be Insured provisions. No conflict identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only a fragment referring to revocable beneficiary and contingent owner survives; no operative rule is legible. Little to construe as written.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the Ownership and Payment of Proceeds provisions and the requirement that a death-proceeds payee be the beneficiary. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The entire-contract/representations clause says statements are representations not warranties and no claim may be denied on a statement unless attached to the contract; that is a clear, standard rule. The "as far as you know and believe" and "good faith" language is qualitative but conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interlocks with Incontestability and with the suicide clause, and in a replacement-policy dispute the attached-application requirement can matter; still no direct contradiction appears. Modest relational weight.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Proceeds payable within 30 days after proof of death; a single definite time limit. No ambiguous term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the insuring agreement's "due proof" requirement and the death proceeds interest provision. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only "one sum unless an option is chosen. We may" survives; the default lump-sum rule is clear even truncated. Nothing genuinely two-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Option definition and the Proceeds Payment Options section. No inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The stated rate is lost to OCR ("at the rate of at Ik per year, but not less than that required by law"), so the interest floor cannot be read from the text alone. The statutory backstop makes the practical result determinate, limiting the ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the Claims 30-day payment rule and the Grace Period deduction of unpaid premiums from proceeds; no contradiction, only sequencing. Low relational risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The incontestability text is broken but conveys a two-year contestable period from date of issue or from any increase, with an exception for nonpayment of premiums; the start date for a replacement policy is the arguable point. judgments.reasoning_cat2: It runs in parallel with the suicide clause's two-year period and with the Contract/representations provision, and in a replacement-policy case whether the period restarts is exactly the harmonisation question. Real but secondary to the suicide clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Requires written notice for choice or change of option, permits the owner to choose while the insured lives, and requires the death-proceeds payee to be the beneficiary. Definite mechanical rules.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the Beneficiary, Payee and Ownership provisions. No conflict identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Proof You Can Be Insured and the other conversion subheadings. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the risk-class footnotes and the Risk Class definition. No inconsistency found.
